message.content:
A **CPU (Central Processing Unit)** and a **GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)** are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for drawing pixels on screen, now also used for highly parallel scientific/ML workloads. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) optimized for low latency, complex branching, and high single‑thread performance. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput; each core does the same operation on many data elements simultaneously. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) with sophisticated control flow, branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution. | Simpler, often SIMD‑style instructions; many cores execute the same instruction stream (SIMT). |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large caches per core (L1/L2/L3), deep memory hierarchy, strong support for random access patterns. | Smaller per‑core cache, relies heavily on fast shared memory and texture caches; best suited for regular, predictable memory accesses. |
| **Typical workloads** | Single‑threaded tasks, operating system services, database queries, web servers, general application code. | Rendering pipelines, video encoding/decoding, physics simulations, machine‑learning inference/training, large‑scale data analytics. |
| **Performance metric** | FLOPS per core * latency* matters more; measured in GHz, IPC (instructions per cycle). | Throughput (FLOPS) dominates; measured in TFLOPs, memory bandwidth. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional imperative programming (C/C++, Java, etc.) with thread libraries (pthreads, OpenMP). | Data‑parallel models (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute shaders); requires explicit parallelization. |

### Why the difference matters

- **Latency vs. throughput**: CPUs excel at low‑latency, unpredictable work; GPUs excel at high‑throughput, predictable work.
- **Energy efficiency**: For a given task, a GPU can finish it faster and thus consume less energy overall, even though its idle power may be higher.
- **Cost & form factor**: CPUs are expensive per core and occupy more silicon area; GPUs pack many cores into a smaller die.

In practice, modern systems use both: the CPU orchestrates tasks and handles serial parts, while the GPU accelerates the heavy, parallel portions. This synergy is why GPUs have become popular beyond graphics—for example, in AI training, scientific simulation, and real‑time ray tracing.
